title: Identifying regions
subtitle: Place in the glass
objectives: Use climate clues to identify regions

steps.title: Climate clues
steps.body: Regions leave marks through climate. Chablis Chardonnay is lean and steely; Californian Chardonnay is riper with more oak. Mosel Riesling is light and off-dry; Clare Valley Riesling is dry with lime. Bordeaux Cabernet is cedar and restraint; Napa is ripe and powerful.

steps.title: Winemaking clues
steps.body: Winemaking traditions also point to regions. American oak's coconut and vanilla suggest traditional Rioja. Long lees ageing and toast suggest Champagne. Carbonic maceration's banana suggests Beaujolais. Dried grape character with high alcohol suggests Amarone. Flor's tangy, nutty character means Fino or Manzanilla.

steps.prompt: Match each clue to its likely region.
steps.explanation: Regional traditions shape flavour as much as grape.

steps.title: Putting it together
steps.body: A lean, mineral, unoaked Chardonnay at 12.5% points to Chablis. A powerful, ripe Cabernet at 14.5% with sweet oak points to Napa. A Sauvignon Blanc with pronounced passion fruit points to Marlborough; with restraint and flint, to Sancerre. Use every clue: climate, grape, winemaking and structure.

steps.prompt: A Sauvignon Blanc with intense passion fruit and grass, very high acidity and no oak. Which region is most likely?
steps.explanation: Pronounced passion fruit and grass with high acidity is classic Marlborough. Sancerre is more restrained; Pessac-Léognan is often oaked.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Climate leaves its mark on the same grape
Combine climate, grape, winemaking and structure
